section_summary: This section documents intensive Japanese military preparations in 1932–1933, including arms and aircraft production, chemical-warfare capacity, strategic railways, public fundraising, troop movements into Manchuria, and contingency planning against the Soviet Union, China, the Philippines, and the United States. Diplomatic and intelligence reports disagree over whether these measures anticipated a specific war or reflected general readiness, and several Chinese-supplied reports contain claims treated skeptically by American officials. The later documents trace growing Japanese political and business opposition to military control, especially criticism of military spending, state indebtedness, and the Army’s influence over foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on Japanese generals and Manchurian preparations
subfiles.about: Reports a senior Japanese general’s arrival and discussions concerning military plans and preparations in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Damaged fragment on flying to Changchun to meet a general from Japan, apparently Mazaki, and on Manchuria-centered military planning.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 96
subfiles.from: M. M. H., Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Recommends reading the attached Tokyo despatch on extraordinary Japanese military preparations.
subfiles.summary: Routing note: the August 13 Tokyo despatch No. 96 shows Japan energetically strengthening its war machine and war psychology, adding to government financial obligations.

subfiles.title: Summary of Tokyo confidential despatch No. 96
subfiles.about: Summarizes material, psychological, financial, and political evidence of Japanese war preparations.
subfiles.summary: Summary of Despatch No. 96: full-time arsenal work, more aircraft, war propaganda, and state borrowing measures; Makino and Ichiki remain conservative opposition; the Embassy sees general readiness rather than a fixed war plan.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 96: Extraordinary Military Preparations in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports extensive material, psychological, financial, and political preparations for war in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew details full-time arsenal production, aircraft and armored-vehicle construction, a chemical-warfare plant at Meguro, replenished reserves, greater imports of strategic materials, and an additional Army appropriation. He describes propaganda by War Minister Araki, patriotic public subscriptions, the expansion of the Bank of Japan’s tax-free fiduciary issue, and military domination following Inukai’s assassination. The despatch considers possible conflict with China or the Soviet Union and a drive into Jehol but concludes that the preparations probably served broad contingency planning.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting Chinese intelligence maps and reports
subfiles.about: Transmits two maps and two memoranda on Japanese military preparations obtained through the Treasury Attaché at Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Fuller says Nicholson received Chinese intelligence maps and reports from an unnamed source, a former Chinese spy in Formosa recently banished.

subfiles.title: Letter acknowledging intelligence enclosure
subfiles.from: W. Baggaley, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of an intelligence enclosure and states that it was copied for Navy files.
subfiles.summary: Captain Baggaley thanks Hornbeck for the very interesting enclosure, which Naval Intelligence copied.

subfiles.title: Japanese Military Preparation for War with Soviet Russia
subfiles.about: Purports to outline a phased Japanese plan for war against the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on Japanese preparation for war with the Soviet Union: control of Manchuria and Mongolia, seizure of the Chinese Eastern Railway, attacks toward Vladivostok and Chita, and occupying northern Sakhalin.

subfiles.title: Japanese Military Preparation for War with the United States
subfiles.about: Purports to describe Japanese bases, resources, and operational plans for a war against the United States.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on preparing for war with the U.S.: Taiwan as a base against the Philippines, planned facilities, occupying the Philippines, and luring the American fleet to a decisive battle near the Ogasawaras.

subfiles.title: Map of Japanese military facilities in Formosa
subfiles.about: Maps locations associated with the accompanying memorandum on Japanese military preparations in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Poorly reproduced map of Japanese military facilities in Taiwan, including the Penghu area and Sun Moon Lake power project.

subfiles.title: Confidential-file endorsement for Navy Department letter
subfiles.about: Records the filing of the September 7 Navy Department letter under 894.20/98.
subfiles.summary: Filing slip placing a September 7, 1932 Navy Department letter in the confidential file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch No. 106
subfiles.about: Directs readers to despatch No. 106 concerning extraordinary military preparations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to despatch No. 106 on extraordinary military preparations in Japan.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2 to despatch No. 106: Japanese military production and readiness
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese armament production, industrial mobilization, public military subscriptions, budgets, maneuvers, and strategic railway construction.
subfiles.summary: The report assembles observations from foreign businessmen and other sources about arsenal activity, aircraft factories, imported machinery, vehicle and tank manufacture, communications equipment, chemical-warfare production, gas masks, naval procurement, and public gifts to the armed forces. It describes new appropriations, intensive maneuvers, foreign weapons purchases, and railway projects linking Korea and Manchuria. The author argues that the pace exceeds ordinary reorganization and suggests that Japan was preparing for a large contingency, most plausibly against the Soviet Union or China, while noting that anti-American propaganda did not necessarily imply an imminent war with the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report No. 111 on Japanese military preparations
subfiles.about: Refers to a report that Japanese military preparations were proceeding with great activity and speed.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's September 1, 1932 report No. 111 on Japanese military preparations.

subfiles.title: Report extract: Military Preparations in Japan
subfiles.about: Condenses evidence of accelerated Japanese military and political preparation.
subfiles.summary: Extract: active arsenals and aircraft factories, round-the-clock Yokosuka work, vehicle and machine-tool purchases, war propaganda and military dominance over civil government; possible aims include the League, Manchuria, China or the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Flimsy report on foreign attachés’ theories of Japanese war preparations
subfiles.about: Reports foreign military attachés’ concern over preparations that might enable Japan to wage a major war.
subfiles.summary: Flimsy report on attachés' theories of Japanese war preparations, from factory work and imports to North Korean railways: a new Russo-Japanese war, readiness against America, or Manchurian operations after the kaoliang is cut.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Japanese troop movements through Dairen
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Dairen despatch reporting substantial and increasingly secret Japanese troop movements.
subfiles.summary: Division summary: troop statistics for June 14 to September 20 show considerable Dairen movement, conducted secretly after the conspicuous midsummer marches.

subfiles.title: Despatch on movement of Japanese troops through Dairen
subfiles.from: E. B. Thomas, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Provides source-based records of Japanese units, personnel, horses, aircraft, artillery, provisions, and ammunition passing through Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Thomas reports Japanese troops moving through Dairen embarked at night and dispersed among ships; a reliable written source lists formations, recruits, horses, aircraft and munitions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram No. 286
subfiles.about: Refers to Grew’s telegram confirming the movement of the Sixth Division to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to telegram No. 286: the War Ministry confirmed the Sixth Division en route to Manchuria to replace the Second.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 286 on deployment of the Sixth Division
subfiles.about: Reports official confirmation that the Japanese Sixth Division was going to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 286: the War Ministry says the Sixth Division, one of Japan's best, is en route to replace the Second Division.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch No. 227
subfiles.about: Refers to Grew’s despatch transmitting Baron Goh’s address on state finances and military expenditure.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to despatch No. 227: Baron Goh's November 24 address to the Tokyo Chamber of Commerce, mainly on public finance and military spending.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 227 transmitting criticism of military expenditure
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Interprets Baron Goh’s financial address and accompanying editorials as evidence of renewed public opposition to Japanese militarism.
subfiles.summary: Grew argues that Goh placed responsibility for Japan’s grave fiscal position directly on military expenditure and probably intended to press the services toward retrenchment. He places the speech within a longer cycle of declining military prestige, wartime enthusiasm after the Manchurian Incident, and renewed concern about taxes, inflation, and debt. The despatch introduces two editorials and an Embassy staff memorandum showing cautious but increasingly visible resistance to military dominance.

subfiles.title: Speech by Baron Goh on Japanese financial policy
subfiles.to: Dinner audience of officials and business leaders
subfiles.about: Warns that deficit financing and largely unproductive military expenditure threatened Japanese financial stability.
subfiles.summary: Goh reviews the widening gap between revenue and expenditure and predicts enormous bond issues, monetary expansion, falling exchange rates, inflation, and possible economic disorder. Although he accepts that Manchurian operations, national defense, and relief measures require spending, he calls military and many public-works expenditures economically unproductive. He urges a fundamental policy to restore sound public finance while protecting genuinely productive enterprises.

subfiles.title: Financial Policy of the Military
subfiles.about: Criticizes military leaders for proposing tax and financial policy outside their proper sphere.
subfiles.summary: The editorial discusses a military proposal to increase taxation on wealthy people and high-dividend companies. It argues that military men should confine themselves to military matters and exercise restraint toward society. The paper warns that overreach could alienate the public and undermine the harmony on which national defense depends.

subfiles.title: Military Authorities and the Political Parties
subfiles.about: Examines reports that Japanese political parties were turning their campaign criticism against the military authorities.
subfiles.summary: Editorial: parties that cannot attack the government or each other now target the military, which may have exceeded its role after Manchuria and risks losing public sympathy.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the League of University Professors of Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a professors’ meeting apparently intended to demonstrate intellectual support for Japan’s overseas policy and the military.
subfiles.summary: Turner reports a League of University Professors gathering that displayed national unity; Professor Inoue privately said culture was neglected for military prowess, suggesting scholars resisted military domination.

subfiles.title: Radiogram on redistribution of Japanese forces
subfiles.about: Reports a War Office plan to strengthen Japanese units in Manchuria by reducing unit strength in Japan proper.
subfiles.summary: Radiogram: the War Office told the Diet on December 27 its force redistribution would materially enlarge forces in Manchuria without proportionate overall Army growth.

subfiles.title: Translation of Nanking cablegram on Japanese mobilization and Chinese constitutionalism
subfiles.from: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nanking, forwarded by the Chinese Legation
subfiles.about: Combines allegations of imminent Japanese mobilization with Kuomintang resolutions on constitutional government.
subfiles.summary: Nanking cablegram: an observer claims Japan's military preparations would be complete in six months, with youth training and mobilization of a million men; also Kuomintang plans for local autonomy and a draft constitution.

subfiles.title: Translation of Nanking cablegram listing Japanese forces in Manchuria
subfiles.from: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nanking, forwarded by the Chinese Legation
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese divisions, brigades, headquarters, and garrisons in the northeastern provinces of China.
subfiles.summary: Nanking cablegram locating elements of five Japanese divisions at points across Manchuria, plus cavalry brigades and an additional Fourth Division said to have come from Korea.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Stimson memorandum on junior-officer control
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Department of State
subfiles.about: Refers to a memorandum in which Stimson recalled saying that younger Army officers controlled the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Stimson's memorandum asserting controlling Japanese officers were no higher than lieutenant colonel.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Stimson memorandum on Tokyo government control
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Department of State
subfiles.about: Refers to a memorandum asserting that young Army officers exercised exceptional control over the government in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Stimson's memorandum contrasting Tokyo with other civilized capitals because its government was said to be in young officers' hands.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 27 on draft reinforcements for Manchuria
subfiles.about: Reports measures expected to increase Japanese enlisted strength in Manchuria by at least one third.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 27: new draftees for Manchurian divisions go there immediately, expiring men are retained, and depot cadres cut; Grew estimates Manchurian enlisted strength rises at least one third.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of telegram on Manchurian reinforcements
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the report that new drafts and extended service would enlarge Japanese forces in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of the War Office's January 23 information on draftee dispatch, retention of soldiers and reduced depot cadres, raising Manchurian strength at least one third.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch No. 271 on opposition to the military
subfiles.about: Refers to a despatch concerning a slowly developing revolt by Japanese political parties against military control.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's January 27 despatch No. 271 on party opposition to military control of the government.

subfiles.title: Summary sheet for despatch No. 271: Opposition to Military in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes Diet interpellations challenging Army influence over Manchuria, foreign policy, and public spending.
subfiles.summary: Summary of Despatch No. 271: Ashida questions the War and Foreign Ministers on the Army's high-handedness; Uchida challenges military budgets and the source of supreme military authority.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 271: Opposition to Military in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Diet criticism of the Army’s conduct in Manchuria, influence over diplomacy, military budgets, and claims of independent supreme command.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes Ashida’s contention that the Army ruled Manchuria by force without a coherent national policy and dominated the Foreign Office. The War and Foreign Ministers denied seeking exclusive control and rejected the charge of a separate War Department diplomacy. Shinya Uchida attacked the scale of Army and Navy budgets and pressed officials on who determined military strength; the War Minister’s invocation of imperial authority reportedly drew laughter and invective in the House.

subfiles.title: Japan Times clipping enclosed with despatch on military opposition
subfiles.to: American Embassy and Department of State
subfiles.about: Prints criticism of Japanese continental diplomacy alongside unrelated news and advertisements.
subfiles.summary: Japan Times clipping urging clearer China and Manchukuo policy and unified diplomacy, discussing Pacific armaments and Soviet security concerns, with other columns on Sven Hedin and film advertisements.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Grew letter on anti-foreign animosity
subfiles.about: Refers to a letter about the deliberate cultivation of Japanese hostility toward foreign nations.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew letter: public animosity against foreign countries was deliberately built up to strengthen the military's Manchurian position.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Japanese Army activities
subfiles.about: Refers to information from a Soviet source concerning activities of the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's March 9, 1933 report on Japanese Army activity from a Soviet source.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Dawson report No. 1180
subfiles.about: Dismisses a report predicting a Japanese attack on the Philippines and the United States.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: Dawson's February 7 report on an impending Japanese attack is a lurid story not worth reading.
